claims.text: A machine-learning model integrating high-throughput DFT phonon calculations with local configurational-disorder descriptors will predict ultra-low phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys more accurately than averaged-property models.
The target materials are compositionally homogeneous, single-phase FCC or BCC high-entropy alloys.
DFT-calculated phonon dispersion relations are useful predictive features for phonon thermal conductivity.
Local structural-disorder metrics are useful predictive features for phonon thermal conductivity.
DFT convergence is sufficiently reliable for the relevant FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy structures.
Local atomic disorder produces enhanced phonon-scattering centers.
High configurational disorder in high-entropy alloys creates abundant phonon-scattering centers.
The phonon-scattering centers created by configurational disorder strongly reduce phonon thermal conductivity.
Correlating DFT phonon-dispersion features and disorder descriptors with experimental conductivity data allows the model to capture the conductivity reduction caused by disorder.
The proposed model will improve prediction accuracy by approximately 20–30% relative to conventional averaged-property models.
Current conventional predictive methods use only averaged mass, bond-strength, and composition data.
The approach is applicable to compositionally homogeneous, single-phase FCC or BCC high-entropy alloys.
Significant nanostructuring may reduce the effectiveness of the approach.
High porosity may reduce the effectiveness of the approach.
Multiphase microstructures may reduce the effectiveness of the approach.
Model performance may vary with the sensitivity of the DFT calculations and the quality of the disorder descriptors.
Laser-flash analysis can provide the phonon thermal-conductivity benchmark used to evaluate the model.
TEM and XRD measurements can verify the local-disorder descriptors used by the model.
The hypothesis is falsified if the model fails to produce a statistically significant reduction of at least 10% in average prediction error relative to conventional methods.
The hypothesis is falsified if the predicted disorder features do not correlate with measured conductivity.

contradictions.description: The principal prediction is a 20–30% accuracy improvement, but the hypothesis is only falsified below a 10% error reduction. An observed improvement between 10% and 20% would miss the stated prediction without satisfying the stated falsification rule.
